standard.title: Types of law
standard.description: the types of law in Australia, including criminal law and civil law, and the place of First Nations Australian customary law
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand the key principles of the Australian legal system including the rule of law and court system (AC9HC7K03), and from K03 in this year level they have developed understanding of the characteristics of laws and how statute, common and delegated law are made. The gap this descriptor fills is the categorical distinctions between types of law in terms of what they regulate and protect — criminal vs civil — and the distinctive place of First Nations customary law within and alongside the Australian legal system.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the types of law in Australia including the fundamental distinction between criminal and civil law and their roles in protecting rights and freedoms, and examine the place of First Nations Australian customary law including through the lens of Native Title.

nodes.label: Criminal law vs civil law
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the fundamental difference between criminal law and civil law, including who initiates legal action, what is at stake and the role of each in protecting rights and freedoms.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the fundamental difference between criminal law and civil law with one example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the fundamental distinction between criminal law (wrongs against society, state prosecutes, criminal sanctions) and civil law (disputes between parties, individual initiates action, civil remedies), and explain the role of each in protecting rights and freedoms.
wider: Investigate a case that involves both criminal and civil dimensions (e.g. assault that results in both a criminal prosecution and a civil damages claim) to examine how the two systems interact
Examine the different standards of proof in criminal and civil law (beyond reasonable doubt vs balance of probabilities) and explain why they differ
Investigate how criminal and civil law operate differently when the 'wrongdoer' is an organisation or corporation rather than an individual
nodes.hinge_reason: The criminal/civil distinction is the structural organiser for the rest of this descriptor and shapes how students understand legal processes, court systems and rights protection throughout K04. A student who cannot distinguish the two categories cannot make sense of where customary law fits or what Native Title protects.

response_modes.reason: The distinction is conceptually clean but often confused by students who conflate 'serious' with 'criminal'. Invest in unpacking the logic of each category — who the wrong is against, who initiates action, and what remedy or sanction applies.

success_criteria: Can explain the key difference between criminal and civil law — including who initiates action and the nature of the outcome
Can give one example each of a criminal law matter and a civil law matter

nodes.label: Distinguishing law types: statutory, common, delegated
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish statutory law, common law and executive (delegated) law from each other, and identify how the houses of parliament can disallow delegated legislation.
nodes.minimum_width: Distinguish statutory law from common law and delegated law with a brief description of each.
nodes.typical_width: Distinguish statutory law (Acts of parliament), common law (judge-made law through precedent) and executive/delegated law (regulations made under parliamentary authority) from each other — explaining the source and authority of each — and identify how the houses of parliament can disallow delegated legislation through disallowance mechanisms.
wider: Trace a specific regulation through the delegated legislation process — identifying the parent Act, the regulation made under it, and whether parliament has used or considered disallowance

Investigate how the three types of law interact in a specific area of Australian law (e.g. environmental law, employment law) — what comes from statute, what from common law, what from delegated regulation
Examine how the balance between statutory, common and delegated law has shifted over time as government regulation has expanded

response_modes.reason: Students built the statute/common law distinction in K03. This node adds delegated law. Widening across examples of all three operating in the same legal domain makes the distinctions more durable.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Seeing all three law types operating in the same legal domain (e.g. environmental or employment law) allows students to understand the legal system as an integrated whole rather than separate categories — building genuine legal literacy.
success_criteria: Can correctly identify the source and authority of statutory, common and delegated law
Can explain how parliament can disallow delegated legislation

nodes.label: First Nations customary law
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the significance of First Nations Australian customary law through selected case studies, explaining what customary law is and how it relates to the broader Australian legal system.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe what First Nations Australian customary law is and explain its significance using at least one case study.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the significance of customary law for First Nations Australians through selected case studies — explaining that customary law comprises the traditional laws, customs and practices of First Nations peoples, and examining how it has been recognised (or not) within the Australian legal system.
wider: Investigate the legal recognition of First Nations customary law in specific Australian jurisdictions, examining where and how courts have incorporated customary law into sentencing or decision-making
Compare how different Australian states and territories have approached the recognition of First Nations customary law, examining arguments for and against greater formal recognition
Investigate case studies from other countries (e.g. New Zealand, Canada) where Indigenous customary law has been given greater formal recognition, and examine what lessons might apply to Australia
nodes.hinge_reason: If students do not understand what customary law is and why it is distinctive, they cannot engage with Native Title — which is specifically about how First Nations Australians' relationship to land, grounded in customary law, is recognised or not by the Australian legal system. A thin treatment here produces students who treat customary law as a historical curiosity rather than a living legal reality.

response_modes.reason: Case studies of customary law recognition across different legal contexts show students that this is not a simple yes/no question. Widening across multiple cases — including those where recognition is partial or contested — builds genuine understanding.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations customary law is both substantively important for Australian civic literacy and analytically rich — it challenges students to examine what counts as law, who has the power to define it and how different legal traditions can coexist. This is a genuinely widening topic with significant pedagogical depth.
success_criteria: Can explain what First Nations Australian customary law is and how it differs from statute or common law
Can describe the significance of customary law to at least one First Nations community or context using a case study

nodes.label: Native Title: opportunities and limitations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the opportunities and limitations of Native Title law for First Nations Australians.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe what Native Title is and identify one opportunity and one limitation it presents for First Nations Australians.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate the opportunities and limitations of Native Title law for First Nations Australians — including what Native Title recognises, the process for claiming it, the conditions under which it is extinguished, and the extent to which it addresses (or does not address) First Nations Australians' rights and relationships to land.
wider: Investigate a specific Native Title claim in Australia, examining the process, evidence required, outcome and significance for the community involved
Analyse the Mabo decision and the Native Title Act 1993 — what they changed, what they left unchanged and the ongoing debates about their adequacy
Examine how Native Title law interacts with state and territory land laws, resource extraction and pastoral leases — and what limitations this creates for First Nations land rights

response_modes.reason: Evaluate is the command term — students need to weigh both sides genuinely. Invest in the evaluative scaffold: what does Native Title offer that didn't exist before, and where does it fall short of full recognition of customary rights?

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Native Title is one of the most contested areas of Australian law and society. Width across different case studies — the Mabo decision, specific NT claims, land-use tensions — allows students to build a genuinely nuanced evaluation rather than a formulaic one.
success_criteria: Can describe what Native Title recognises and how it is claimed
Can identify at least one concrete opportunity and one concrete limitation of Native Title law for First Nations Australians
